issues.legal_issue: A partnership remained in existence when an agreement was made in its name, so the signatory acted as a partner rather than as its sole proprietor.
material_facts: The agreement identified the signatory as a partner, including in the counterpart produced by the opposing side; the description was struck out in the signatory’s copy without initials.
A purported dissolution deed used stamp paper that was not printed until after the date the deed bore, and the signatory resisted efforts to verify the stamp paper’s date of issue.
No written notice of the alleged retirement was given to the contracting business, and no public notice was published.
The signatory continued to conduct partnership transactions after the date on which dissolution was alleged to have occurred.
issues.conclusion: The partnership was not shown to have been dissolved on the alleged date, and the agreement was entered into by the signatory as a partner.
issues.legal_principle: The court determined the partnership’s status and the signatory’s capacity from the documents, the circumstances surrounding the purported dissolution deed, and the parties’ conduct. It considered the absence of notice of a partner’s retirement relevant because persons dealing with the firm might otherwise assume that the partnership continued.

rule.if: agreement_identifies_signatory_as_partner and (purported_dissolution_document_has_inconsistent_provenance or partnership_transactions_continued) and retirement_notice_was_not_given

predicates.agreement_identifies_signatory_as_partne: The agreement or its counterpart described the signatory as a partner of the business.
predicates.purported_dissolution_document_has_incon: The person asserting dissolution relied on a dissolution document whose production circumstances or materials were inconsistent with its stated date.
predicates.partnership_transactions_continued: The alleged retiring partner continued to conduct transactions for the partnership after the asserted dissolution date.
predicates.retirement_notice_was_not_given: The alleged retiring partner did not notify the persons dealing with the partnership or the public of the retirement.

issues.definition: When an agreement identifies its signatory as a partner and the claimed dissolution is undermined by the document’s provenance, continuing transactions, and lack of retirement notice, the agreement is treated as made in the signatory’s capacity as a partner.

issues.legal_issue: A partner cannot bring a suit on behalf of an unregistered firm to enforce a contractual right, except where the suit falls within the statutory exception for rights concerning dissolution or realization of a dissolved firm’s property.
material_facts: The firm was not registered under the Partnership Act.
The agreement sued upon had been made by the plaintiff as a partner of that firm.
The suit sought to enforce rights arising from the agreement for the benefit of the firm.
The plaintiff did not plead that he was suing to recover the outstanding property or dues of a dissolved firm.
issues.conclusion: The suit was barred by Section 69 of the Partnership Act and was not maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: Section 69(2) of the Partnership Act bars a suit by or on behalf of an unregistered firm to enforce a contractual right against a third party. Section 69(3) extends the bar to other proceedings to enforce contractual rights, while Section 69(3)(a) preserves proceedings to enforce a right to realize the property of a dissolved firm. The provision is mandatory, and the court treated a partner’s suit enforcing a contract made for an unregistered firm as a suit on behalf of that firm.

rule.if: suit_to_enforce_firm_contract against_third_party and firm_is_unregistered and plaintiff_acts_for_firm and not suit_seeks_realization_of_dissolved_firm_property

predicates.suit_to_enforce_firm_contract: The proceeding is a suit seeking to enforce a contractual right undertaken for a firm.
predicates.against_third_party: The suit is brought against a person outside the firm.
predicates.firm_is_unregistered: The firm had not been registered when the contractual right was sought to be enforced.
predicates.plaintiff_acts_for_firm: The plaintiff brings the claim for the benefit or interest of the firm.
predicates.suit_seeks_realization_of_dissolved_firm: The suit seeks to enforce a right to realize property of a dissolved firm.

issues.definition: A suit by or for an unregistered firm against a third party to enforce a firm contract is barred unless it seeks to realize the property of a dissolved firm.

issues.legal_issue: A partner who sues to recover partnership dues that include amounts belonging to the partnership cannot maintain the suit without joining the other partner whose interests are involved.
material_facts: The plaintiff alone brought the suit to recover an amount that included items due to the partnership.
The other partner was not joined, despite an objection that he was a necessary party.
The suit was brought by the plaintiff as the person claiming the partnership dues.
issues.conclusion: Even assuming the statutory bar did not apply, the plaintiff could not maintain the suit without joining the other partner.
issues.legal_principle: A person seeking recovery of partnership amounts that include dues belonging to the partnership cannot maintain the claim alone when another partner has an interest in those amounts; that partner is a necessary party.

predicates.suit_to_recover_partnership_dues: The proceeding is a suit to recover amounts claimed as partnership dues.
predicates.claim_includes_partnership_items: The amount claimed includes items that are due to the partnership rather than solely to the individual plaintiff.
predicates.other_interested_partner_not_joined: A partner with an interest in the amounts claimed was not made a party to the suit.

issues.definition: A suit to recover partnership dues that include partnership items cannot be maintained by one partner alone when another interested partner has not been joined.

issues.legal_issue: An unconsented material alteration to a deed that changes the parties’ rights or legal position renders the deed ineffective against a party who did not consent to the change.
material_facts: The suit sought to enforce a written financial agreement.

The plaintiff’s copy differed from the counterpart produced by the defendants in several respects: a reference to the plaintiff as a partner was removed, a payment deadline was changed, and wording governing commission was altered.
The court found that the changes materially varied the parties’ rights, liabilities, or legal position and were made without the defendants’ consent.
issues.conclusion: The material alterations made without the defendants’ consent had the effect of cancelling the deed, rendering it void as a basis for the suit.
issues.legal_principle: A material alteration is one that varies the parties’ rights, liabilities, or legal position, changes the instrument’s legal effect, or otherwise prejudices a party bound by the deed as originally executed. An alteration of that kind made without the consent of the party bound renders the deed void against that party. The court relied on Halsbury’s Laws of England, Volume 12, paragraph 1378, and the Privy Council decision in Nahtu Lal v. Musamat Gomti.

predicates.suit_seeks_enforcement_of_written_deed: The proceeding seeks to enforce a written deed against a party to it.
predicates.deed_was_materially_altered: The deed was changed in a way that varied the parties’ rights, liabilities, legal position, or the instrument’s legal effect.
predicates.alteration_was_without_consent_of_party_: The material change was made without the consent of the party against whom the deed is sought to be enforced.

issues.definition: A deed sought to be enforced against a party is void against that party when it was materially altered without that party’s consent.

issues.legal_issue: A court cannot award a specific sum by independently examining accounts when the plaintiff sued on the basis that the accounts had been settled and the alleged settlement was not proved.
material_facts: The plaintiff sued for a specific, ascertained sum on the asserted basis that the accounts had been settled.
The courts below found that no settlement of accounts had taken place as alleged.
The courts nevertheless examined the accounts and awarded an amount they considered due, without allowing the defendants to challenge the items through an accounting process.
issues.conclusion: After finding no settlement of accounts, the courts should have dismissed the suit or passed a preliminary decree for accounts allowing the defendants to challenge the items; they should not have made out a new case and awarded an amount on their own examination of the accounts.
issues.legal_principle: When a plaintiff sues for a fixed sum on the basis of a stated or settled account and the alleged settlement is not proved, the court may not substitute an unpleaded accounting claim and determine the amount itself. The proper course is to dismiss the suit or direct an accounting in which the entries can be examined and impeached for fraud, mistake, inaccuracy, or omission; such errors may include errors of law as well as errors of fact.

predicates.suit_for_fixed_sum_on_settled_account: The plaintiff brings a suit for a specific sum on the asserted basis that the accounts were stated or settled.
predicates.alleged_account_settlement_not_proved: The court finds that the account settlement alleged by the plaintiff did not occur.
predicates.court_awards_sum_from_its_own_account_ex: The court examines the account itself and awards a sum without directing a proper accounting process in which the opposing party can challenge the entries.

issues.definition: When a fixed-sum suit rests on a settlement that is not proved, the court must dismiss the suit or order an accounting rather than award a sum based on its own account examination.

issues.legal_issue: Persons who take or use charged business assets are not personally liable for the secured debt when the charged assets remain available to satisfy it and dissipation of those assets is not established.
material_facts: The plaintiff claimed a charge over the business assets and sought to impose liability on persons who later dealt with the business and its goods.
The receivers obtained possession of the charged properties that existed before the later business arrangement.
The evidence did not establish that those properties had been removed or dissipated through conversion or detention.
The charged goods remained available to satisfy any liability secured by the charge.
issues.conclusion: The later business participants could not be held personally liable for the decretal amount because the charged goods remained available for satisfaction of the claim and their removal or dissipation was not established.
issues.legal_principle: The court upheld the determination that persons who intermeddle with charged goods are not personally liable for the secured amount where the charged property remains available for recovery and no removal or dissipation of it is proved.

predicates.proceeding_seeks_personal_liability_of_l: The proceeding seeks to impose personal liability on persons who later handled or used business assets subject to a charge.
predicates.charged_assets_remain_available: The charged assets remain in the custody of a receiver or otherwise available to satisfy the secured claim.
predicates.dissipation_of_charged_assets_not_proved: The claimant has not established that the charged assets were removed, converted, or dissipated.

issues.definition: Persons later handling charged assets are not personally liable for the secured debt when the assets remain available and their dissipation has not been proved.
